newsitem.title: VATICAN: Taiwan Vice-President invites Pope to visit island.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan Vice-President invites Pope to visit island.

text.p: Taiwan's Vice-President Lien Chan invited Pope John Paul on Tuesday to visit the island, which China considers a rebel province, and said the Pontiff had agreed to consider the offer.
"I invited His Holiness to visit my country, particularly during his future pastoral trips (to Asia and the Pacific)," Lien told a news conference after the 35-minute audience.
"He said he will consider our proposal," Lien, the highest-ranking Taiwanese official to visit the Vatican, said.
Lien would not be drawn on whether he and the Pope had discussed Beijing's criticism of the Vatican and the status of Chinese Catholics on the communist mainland.
"We did review the general situation, not only in Asia but worldwide," he said, declining to respond specifically.
The Vatican is the only state in Europe which has diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
The audience irked Beijing, which does not allow its Catholics to recognise the Pope and insists that the Vatican break ties with Taiwan if it wants improved relations.
Lien said he was confident that good relations with the Vatican would continue. He said he had asked the Pope "to pray for my country" and the Pontiff said he would.
"We have shared goals, ideals and values and I firmly believe that our relationship (with the Vatican) will continue to be friendly, close and mutually beneficial one," he said.
In Beijing, a foreign ministry spokesman told the Holy See not to interfere when asked about the meeting.
Lien said the meeting had been very warm and cordial and that he and the Pope had discussed bilateral relations and international issues, particularly Asia.
Lien said Taiwan had given the Pope a charitable contribution of $1 million during the audience.

The Vatican said the Pope had passed along the gift to "Cor Unum", the department that oversees the Church charitable works, and that it would be used to help reconstruction in Bosnia and the Great Lakes region in Africa.
Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said he had no commment on Beijing's recent criticism of the Vatican.
China was upset by a papal statement on Monday that the Vatican would closely watch how Catholics in Hong Kong were treated after the British colony is handed over to Beijing in July.

"We would hope to have no interference in our religious affairs, and when we talk about interference, the scope is very wide, not only including missionary work but also in appointments of bishops," a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said.
Catholics on the Chinese mainland who want to worship openly must belong to the state-controlled Chinese Catholic Patriotic Association. Those loyal to the Pope worship secretly.
China's Catholic and Protestant churches, both tightly controlled by the state, claim several million believers but many more are thought to worship at underground churches.
Authorities view underground congregations as a threat to party rule.

The U.S.-based church group Cardinal Kung Foundation said last week that officials in Chongren county in the central Jiangxi province had issued an action plan to stamp out worship by the underground Catholic church loyal to Rome.
